title: 5 Steps to Get Out of a Debt Trap
summary: A debt trap is borrowing again to meet what you owe. See a worked Pune example, avalanche vs snowball, loan consolidation and your rights if you miss EMIs.
body_markdown:
A debt trap is a cycle in which you borrow again to keep up with what you already owe, so the total keeps growing even though you pay every month. Getting out means stopping new borrowing, paying more than the minimums, and choosing an order for your debts.


## What is a debt trap?


A debt trap is a cycle in which loan EMIs and card dues take so much of your income that you borrow again to cover them, and the new borrowing adds to next month's bill. An EMI (equated monthly instalment) is the fixed amount you pay each month that covers interest and part of the loan.


Take Rohan, a 29-year-old sales executive in Pune. His take-home pay, what reaches his account after deductions, is ₹55,000 a month. His debts and the loan rates are assumed for the example.


- A credit card balance of ₹80,000.
- A personal loan with ₹1,50,000 left, at an assumed 14% a year, with an EMI of ₹7,202 for the remaining 24 months.
- A consumer-durable loan with ₹30,000 left, at an assumed 16% a year, with an EMI of ₹2,722 for the remaining 12 months.


The card's minimum amount due is ₹4,600 this month. Minimum amount due is the smallest part of the bill a cardholder must pay so that the bill is not treated as overdue. For this example it is worked out on SBI Card's published terms (read October 2026), which charge 3.75% a month, or 45% a year, on an unsecured card's carried balance. Its minimum due includes the month's interest and charges plus 2% of the remaining balance; this example leaves out GST and fees. Here that is ₹3,000 plus ₹1,600.


Add the two EMIs and Rohan owes about ₹14,524 a month in minimum payments. Now a surprise bill, say for a repair or a hospital visit, goes on the card. It joins a balance that is already charged 3.75% a month. Next month's bill is bigger. The 3.75% is SBI Card's published term, not a market rate.


### Is all debt a trap?


No. Whether a debt turns into a trap depends on the interest rate, what the money buys and whether the payments fit your income.


## How do you know you are in a debt trap?


The warning signs are paying only the card minimum, using one loan or card to pay another, missing or delaying EMIs, and EMIs taking a growing share of your take-home pay.


A quick check is the EMI-to-income ratio: your EMIs plus card minimum payments, divided by take-home pay. For Rohan it is ₹14,524 divided by ₹55,000, which is 26.4%. Lenders apply limits of their own, covered in[why personal loans get rejected](https://koshex.com/blog/common-reasons-for-personal-loan-rejection-tips-to-avoid) .


## How do you get out of a debt trap, step by step?


You get out by listing every debt, adding no new credit, fixing a monthly amount for repayment, paying every minimum on time, and putting the rest on one debt at a time. In order:


1. **List every debt.** Write the balance, the interest rate, the EMI and the due date for each.
2. **Make a budget.** A budget is a plan for what you will spend and what you will keep aside each month.[The money management guide](https://koshex.com/blog/the-ultimate-guide-to-money-management) and[tracking your expenses](https://koshex.com/blog/track-your-personal-expenses) cover how.
3. **Stop new borrowing.** Otherwise the balance grows back.
4. **Automate payments.** So no EMI or minimum is missed by accident.
5. **Pick an order for the extra money.** The next section compares two.
6. **Review every month.**


The fixed amount matters. In Rohan's case, paying only the minimums closes the two loans on schedule, in 12 and 24 months. The card balance, though, falls by only 2% a month. After five years about ₹23,804 would still be owed on it, and interest across the three debts would come to about ₹1,30,876, with no new spending. RBI makes card issuers print a warning on every bill that paying only the minimum stretches repayment over months or years, with compounded interest.


## Which debt should you pay off first?


The avalanche method pays the debt with the highest interest rate first and costs less interest. The snowball method pays the smallest balance first and closes an account sooner.


Suppose Rohan spends ₹33,000 a month on essentials, an assumed figure, which leaves ₹22,000 a month for debts. Nothing new is borrowed.


Method Order First account cleared Debt-free in Total interest


Avalanche Card, then consumer loan, then personal loan Month 8 (card) 14 months about ₹32,398


Snowball Consumer loan, then card, then personal loan Month 3 (consumer loan) 14 months about ₹35,935


On these figures, the avalanche costs about ₹3,537 less interest. The snowball closes its first account five months sooner than the avalanche closes its first.


### Can you be debt-free in a year?


It depends on the balances, the rates and the monthly amount. On Rohan's figures, ₹22,000 a month clears everything in 14 months, not 12.


## Should you combine your debts into one loan?


Combining debts into one new loan, which is called consolidation, helps only if the new loan's total cost, interest plus every fee, is lower than what you pay now. It also works only if you stop using the cards you cleared. A card balance transfer is checked the same way: compare its total cost, interest plus every fee.


Take Rohan's card balance alone. Repaying ₹80,000 over 12 equal monthly payments at 3.75% a month costs ₹8,401 a month and ₹20,812 in interest. Suppose he instead takes an ₹80,000 personal loan for 12 months at an assumed 14% a year. The EMI is ₹7,183 and the interest ₹6,196. The lender also charges an assumed processing fee of 2%, a charge for setting up the loan, which is ₹1,600. The total cost is ₹7,796.


On these assumptions the loan costs about ₹13,016 less. That holds only if the card is not used again and the lender's real rate and fee match the assumed ones.


### What should you check before you sign?


Before you sign a personal, home or other retail loan, the lender must give you a Key Facts Statement (KFS), in a standard format and a language you understand. It shows the loan amount, the rate, every fee, the repayment schedule and the APR, which is the yearly cost of the loan including those fees. RBI's method takes the monthly rate of return on the money you actually receive, multiplied by 12. In the example, ₹78,400 reaches Rohan after the fee, and the APR is 17.87%. Compare APRs, not EMIs.


You get at least three working days to accept the loan on those terms. A fee that is not in the KFS cannot be charged later unless you explicitly agree to it. These rules cover retail loans sanctioned on or after 1 October 2024. Credit card dues are exempt.


### Can you prepay the new loan?


Prepayment means paying a loan off early, in part or in full. If your loan is on a floating rate and you took it as an individual for a purpose other than business, the lender cannot charge you for prepaying it, from any source of money and at any time. A floating rate can change during the loan.


On a fixed-rate loan the lender may charge what its policy and your loan papers say, worked out on the amount you prepay. In RBI's terms a fixed rate is fixed for the whole loan. Check which kind you have.


## Should you use savings or investments to clear expensive debt?


It can cut the interest you pay, but it uses money you set aside for goals or emergencies. Selling mutual fund units can also bring tax and exit loads, which is a fee some funds charge if you sell within a set time after buying. Borrowing against your investments keeps them, but it is still a loan.


RBI lets a bank lend up to 75% of the value of your equity or hybrid fund units and up to 85% of your debt fund units, and banks often lend less.[Get a loan against mutual funds](https://koshex.com/blog/get-loan-against-mutual-funds) compares that with a personal loan and[selling](https://koshex.com/blog/should-i-redeem-my-funds-since-the-markets-are-down) . Most banks also lend against your own fixed deposit without breaking it, as[loans against fixed deposits](https://koshex.com/blog/do-banks-offer-loans-against-fixed-deposits) explains.


Whether to clear debt or invest is a trade-off with its own assumptions.[Prepay your home loan or invest](https://koshex.com/blog/prepay-home-loan-or-invest) weighs it, including card and personal loans.


## What if you cannot pay your EMIs?


Tell the lender before the EMI is missed and ask what it can offer. A missed EMI can bring a penal charge and shows on your credit report.


### What happens when you miss an EMI?


A penal charge is a late-payment charge. RBI's rules say it is charged on the overdue amount, disclosed in your loan agreement and Key Facts Statement, and is not extra interest added to your rate. No interest can be charged on the penalty itself. Interest keeps running on the unpaid EMI at your normal loan rate.


The loan is overdue from the day an EMI is missed. If instalments stay unpaid for more than 90 days, the loan becomes a non-performing asset (NPA) in the bank's books, which shows on your credit report. Lenders must alert you by SMS or email when they report a default or days past due.[What are EMIs and how do they work](https://koshex.com/blog/what-are-emis-and-how-do-they-work) covers missed EMIs in full.


### What can a recovery agent do?


A recovery agent is a person or firm a lender appoints to collect overdue money. Even if you fall behind, RBI bars the lender and its agents from intimidation or harassment of any kind. That includes shaming you in public, pulling in your family, friends or references, sending inappropriate messages, making threatening or anonymous calls, and calling before 8 am or after 7 pm. For card dues, RBI's card rules allow recovery calls only between 10 am and 7 pm.


The lender must tell you which agency it has appointed, and the agent must carry an authorisation letter and identity card. The lender is responsible for what its agents do. Threats or morphed photos are also crimes you can report to the police, through 1930 or[cybercrime.gov.in](https://cybercrime.gov.in/) .


### Where can you complain?


Complain to the lender first, through the grievance officer named in your Key Facts Statement or on the app. If it does not reply within 30 days, or you are not satisfied, you can complain free of charge to the RBI Ombudsman, RBI's complaints service for regulated lenders, at[cms.rbi.org.in](https://cms.rbi.org.in/) . This covers banks, most NBFCs and credit bureaus. For a housing finance company, go to the National Housing Bank's GRIDS portal after one month instead.


### Does settling a loan end the problem?


Settlement closes the debt but leaves a mark. "Settled" means the lender accepted less than you owed because you could not pay in full. "Closed" means you paid everything. Lenders read "settled" as a warning, and a bank that settles with you must wait at least 12 months before lending to you again, except on farm loans.[Why your CIBIL score is low](https://koshex.com/blog/reasons-for-having-a-low-cibil-score-how-to-improve-it) explains what it does to a score.


## How do you keep a small buffer while you repay?


Keeping a little cash aside while you repay stops the next surprise bill from going on a card. An emergency fund is money kept aside for sudden costs such as a job loss or a hospital bill.


How much to keep, and where, is covered in[Where to keep your emergency savings](https://koshex.com/blog/where-should-you-keep-your-emergency-savings) , which puts it at three to six months of expenses.
